title: Slowing AI Down Is a PR Blunder; Cyberattacks Are the Real Risk
dek: Frontier labs packaging safety as pacing pleases no one; what's actually urgent is that CVE weaponization has gone from years to minutes, while enterprises still have no agents, only faster search.
why: The Databricks CEO lays out pacing, the RSI test, the cyberattack curve, enterprise agent adoption and cost governance in one pass; the mechanics of ontology and harness in the back half are the most valuable part.
who: Founders, investors and engineers watching AI safety narratives, enterprise agent adoption and cost governance, especially anyone building agent products.
skip: The pacing PR discussion from 0:00-7:17 can be fast-forwarded; the core mechanics are in the back half.

points.h: Pacing is a PR blunder, not a safety strategy
points.body: Ali argues that frontier labs packaging "safety" as "pacing" is a textbook PR blunder. Pacing is orthogonal to safety — you can build weapons slowly, and that's no different from building weapons; and these companies have been running at full speed and buying more compute, so nobody believes the pacing talk. The result pleases no one: doomers think it isn't a pause, and policy people think you don't know how to do it at all. What they should be saying, he argues, is "secure the frontier," not "pace the frontier."

points.h: RSI only counts if four conditions hold at once
points.body: Ali gives four criteria for judging whether recursive self-improvement is happening, and all must hold simultaneously: the next-generation model needs fewer resources (GPUs) to train, takes less time to train, is smarter/more accurate, and these three things can repeat over and over. If any one fails, the system self-limits — for instance, with constant resources it hits a hardware wall. He stresses that "software writing software" is already happening, with more than 90% of software at Databricks written by AI, but that is not the same as superintelligence.

points.h: The cost curve for frontier training runs the other way
points.body: Sarah points out that the compute bar for training frontier models keeps rising, from 100 million to 1 billion, and now roughly 5 to 10 billion. Ali adds: there are only one or two such training runs a year, and they flatly violate those four criteria — they need more resources, more people, are more fragile, and require building data centers, networking and better fault tolerance. Several have blown up, and failure means burning enormous sums. So the reality is "slower, more fragile, harder," not "faster, cheaper, smarter."

points.h: Weaponization time for a vulnerability went from two or three years to hours
points.body: Ali gives this curve: in 2018 and 2019, a CVE took roughly two to three years from disclosure to weaponization; by 2022 it was down to eight or nine months; from 2022 to now it has compressed to basically hours, almost no time at all. The reason is that data and AI are merging with the cybersecurity market — companies run large numbers of agents internally, generating massive logs and traces, and the volume of data that needs analyzing is orders of magnitude larger than a year or two ago.

points.h: Say AI will destroy the world, then ask if you want IPO allocation
points.body: Ali concedes two things can be true at once: some people really are scared by AI risk, and some people want regulation to "pace us" — because slowing down benefits them. He says people can always reconcile self-interest and fear into a harmonious whole in their own heads. The industry has long had this marketing move: the moment a new model is trained, shout about how terrifyingly good it is, and the world's attention arrives. But he also gives the other side: the time from CVE to actual weaponized exploit went from years to minutes in three or four years, and cyberattacks are real. So "scary" is both a genuine risk and excellent marketing.

points.h: Enterprises have no agents, only faster search
points.body: Ali polled the room on the spot: he asked how many in the audience were managing hundreds or thousands of agents coordinating and negotiating with each other, and almost no hands went up. Most enterprises use Microsoft Copilot, which is essentially a chatbot — "a very, very glorified efficient Google search." Coding is the only scenario that has truly landed, and even its ROI is debatable. He thinks the reason isn't that models aren't smart enough, but that models lack the organization's internal context: they haven't sat in every meeting, don't know what's in everyone's head, don't know the processes. Every organization has a few employees who know everything, and when you tap them on the shoulder you think, "what if he quits?" Pour that context into today's frontier models and you get enormous productivity, and that doesn't require a smarter model.

points.h: Ontology is that employee who's been there five years
points.body: Ali explains ontology with a concrete picture: two people equally smart, equally hardworking, with identical educational backgrounds — one on their first day, one who's been there five years. The difference is that the latter knows how the organization runs, who people are, how things get done — "don't look at the org chart, don't ask that guy, he can't get anything done." That is ontology, the tacit knowledge scattered across everyone's heads. He contrasts it with the state of agents today: today's agentic loop looks up resources one at a time, like Google crawling ten sites live on every search, taking ten minutes, and then handing you ten blue links — expensive, slow and bad. Google's answer was the index, and AI also needs that index computed offline, only harder — because of permission constraints, since data I can access isn't necessarily data you can access, and the object types go far beyond web pages.

points.h: Same model, different harness, nearly 2x the cost
points.body: Databricks's answer is a whole cost-governance stack: Unity Gateway provides token capacity for OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, Grok and open-source models, sets budget caps and alerts by person and by group, does cost forecasting analytics, and adds intelligent routing to switch to cheaper models when nearing budget or when the question is simple. Ali gives a concrete number: the same model, the same version, just a different harness, and actual cost can differ by nearly 2x. Their in-house harness is called Omnigent, which can multiplex across different harnesses. The result is that token usage keeps rising while AI cost stays roughly flat.
